1289.title: Heedlessness, the forgetting
1289.hook: forgetting Allah in the rush of the day
1289.howItsDone: Muslims counter ghaflah, heedlessness, with dhikr, the remembrance of Allah, built into the day through the prayers, the call to prayer, and short remembrances said on waking, eating and leaving home.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the road of lying, and your line: truth leads to good. Truth after truth becomes a road.

Alarm. Coffee. Inbox. Car. Meeting. Lunch at the desk. Another meeting. Traffic. Dinner. Phone. Sleep. Nothing in that day was wrong. No one was lied to, nobody was envied, no temper was lost. And still, somewhere in it, what the Qur'an calls heedlessness may have happened. It isn't a sin anyone sets out to commit. It's a remembering that gets skipped, all day, without anyone noticing. Today's word: ghaflah, heedlessness, the forgetting.
screen: `A DAY WITH NOTHING WRONG.` → `A REMEMBERING SKIPPED.` → `GHAFLAH.`

segments.voice: Start with a verse that names the cure and the disease together. The Qur'an tells the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, to remember his Lord within himself, humbly and with awe, at morning and evening, and it ends, in Pickthall's words: "And be not thou of the neglectful." The Arabic word there is al-ghafilin, the heedless. Morning and evening: the edges of the day, the very times a rush begins and ends. Second, what forgetting does. Another verse warns against being like those who forgot Allah, so that he made them forget themselves. Forgetting Allah isn't a small gap on a schedule; it comes with losing track of your own soul. Third, a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari puts it starkly: the one who remembers his Lord and the one who doesn't are like the living and the dead. Not good and bad. Awake and not. And last, the cure, which you first met as the heart's polish on day three hundred eight. Heedlessness isn't fixed by one long session. It's fixed by small bells through the day: the call to prayer, the words said on waking, before eating, on leaving the house. Each one is a tap on the shoulder, for a day that, left alone, forgets.
screen: `AT MORNING AND EVENING.` · `FORGOT ALLAH, FORGOT THEMSELVES.` · `THE LIVING AND THE DEAD.` · then, large: `SMALL BELLS THROUGH THE DAY.`

segments.voice: Picture the busiest part of today and give it a small reminder, a phone alarm or a sticky note, with one word on it: Allah, or wake up, or something you're grateful for. Decide what you'll do when it comes: one breath, one line of a remembrance you already know, one look out a window. If you pray, you can ask not to be among the heedless.
Ghaflah. Heedlessness: forgetting Allah in the rush of the day; in the Qur'an, the neglectful. Today's word.
Your line: wake up. The living and the dead, the hadith says: awake and not. Tomorrow, the last disease of the heart: despair.

1290.title: Despair, the closed door
1290.hook: no one despairs of Allah's mercy except those without faith (12:87)
1290.howItsDone: Muslim teachers treat despair of Allah's mercy as a disease of the heart, citing Jacob's words in Surah Yusuf and the call of Qur'an 39:53 to those who have wronged themselves not to despair.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ghaflah, heedlessness, and your line: wake up. Small bells through the day.

A father at home, waiting. In Surah Yusuf, Jacob has lost his son Joseph, and now a second son is held far away in Egypt. The Qur'an says his eyes went white with grief. If anyone has a reason to close the door, it's him. Instead he turns to his other sons and sends them back out on the road: go, look for news of Joseph and his brother. Then he says the line this day is built on. Today: despair, the closed door.
screen: `A GRIEVING FATHER.` → `EYES WHITE WITH SORROW.` → `GO, LOOK FOR NEWS.`

segments.voice: Here is what Jacob says, in Pickthall's words: "despair not of the Spirit of Allah. Lo! none despaireth of the Spirit of Allah save disbelieving folk." First, who is speaking. Not someone with a comfortable life handing out advice, but a man whose grief has taken his sight, telling his sons to keep looking. You met his tears on day one hundred thirty-one. Grief isn't despair; he wept and kept looking. Hope, in this story, isn't a mood. It's getting back on the road. Second, despair is called a disease of the heart because of what it claims: this is beyond Allah's mercy. That's a claim about Allah, and in the verse it sits next to unbelief. Third, a verse first met on day five hundred fifty-nine, and again on the day of fear and hope, which opens the door wider still: "Say: O My slaves who have been prodigal to their own hurt! Despair not of the mercy of Allah, Who forgiveth all sins." People who have wasted a great deal, on themselves, addressed by name. And last, a look back over these diseases: arrogance, envy, showing off, anger, greed, backbiting, lying, heedlessness, and now despair. Each had a cure: a correction accepted, a prayer, a hidden deed, a seat, enough, silence, a true sentence, a reminder. Despair says none of it will work. The verse says the door stays open. And if the darkness ever turns toward hurting yourself, in the US call or text 988, any hour; elsewhere, local emergency help. Tell someone you trust.
screen: `DESPAIR NOT OF THE SPIRIT OF ALLAH.` · `A CLAIM ABOUT ALLAH'S MERCY.` · `PRODIGAL TO THEIR OWN HURT.` · then, large: `THE DOOR STAYS OPEN.`

segments.voice: Let one hard thing come to mind, just one: a relationship, a habit, a diagnosis, a debt, something you've decided won't change, and hold it the way Jacob held his lost son, honestly, without pretending it doesn't hurt. Then do what he did and send someone back out on the road: one small step of looking, one question, one call, one try. If you pray, you can ask Allah for help with it by name; if not, just leave the door open a crack.
Despair. Giving up hope of Allah's mercy; in Surah Yusuf, the closed door a grieving father refuses to close. Today's word.
Your line: never despair. That closes the diseases of the heart. Tomorrow, a new part begins: what adab means.

1291.title: What adab means
1291.hook: adab is courtesy toward Allah, people and things
1291.howItsDone: Muslims learn adab, the manners of daily life, from the Prophet's example: saying bismillah before eating, eating with the right hand and from what is nearest, greeting, and treating people, animals and things with care.

segments.voice: Yesterday, despair, and your line: never despair. That closed the diseases of the heart.

A boy is eating at the Prophet's table, and his hand is wandering all over the shared dish, reaching here, reaching there. Sahih al-Bukhari keeps the moment, told by the boy himself, Umar ibn Abi Salamah, who was being raised in the Prophet's household. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, doesn't scold him or send him away. He gives him three short instructions. And with them, a new part of the path begins: manners, and the word that holds them. Today: adab.
screen: `A HAND ALL OVER THE DISH.` → `NO SCOLDING.` → `ADAB.`

segments.voice: Here's what he told the boy: young man, say the name of Allah, eat with your right hand, and eat from what is in front of you. Three instructions, reaching in three directions. Saying Allah's name is courtesy toward Allah. Eating from what's in front of you, not reaching across everyone's side, is courtesy toward the people at the table. And the right hand is a habit for the body itself, the way the meal is held. Adab is the word for that whole web: manners, courtesy, the right way to be with Allah, with people, and with things. Second, why it isn't small. The Qur'an praises the Prophet's character in one line, met back on day six hundred forty-one, in Pickthall's words: "And lo! thou art of a tremendous nature." Manners aren't decoration on top of faith; they're how character shows up at a table. Third, courtesy reaches past people. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says Allah has prescribed excellence in everything, and gives a hard example: when you slaughter, sharpen the blade and spare the animal. Things and creatures are owed courtesy too. And last, the boy. In al-Bukhari's report, he says that was how he ate from then on. Not a rule memorized. A habit given gently, at the right moment, that stayed.
screen: `SAY THE NAME, RIGHT HAND, NEAR SIDE.` · `TOWARD ALLAH, PEOPLE AND THINGS.` · `OF A TREMENDOUS NATURE.` · then, large: `EXCELLENCE IN EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: Choose one ordinary thing you'll do today and picture doing it with adab, slowly, with care. A meal begun with the name of Allah, if that's yours to say, eaten from your own side; a door held and closed gently; a borrowed book put back the way you found it; a message answered with a greeting first. If you pray, you can ask for good manners.
Adab. Courtesy and good manners toward Allah, people and things; the right way to do an ordinary thing. Today's word.
Your line: courtesy in everything. Toward Allah, people and things. See you tomorrow, for the manners of the tongue.

1292.title: Adab of speech
1292.hook: say good or keep silent: the manners of the tongue start in the gap before a word
1292.howItsDone: Muslim teachers cite the hadith "say good or keep silent" when they teach the manners of speech, often alongside the Qur'an's call to speak the kindlier word.

segments.voice: Yesterday, adab: courtesy toward Allah, toward people, toward things. Your line: courtesy in everything.

A reply sits half typed. The cursor blinks. It's sharp, it's accurate, and it would land. Your thumb hovers over send. Between the thought and the word there's a gap about one breath wide, and a lot happens in it. The manners of speech in Islam begin right there, with a short line from the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. It ties the way a person talks to faith itself, and it offers exactly two choices. Neither of them is the sharp reply.
screen: `A REPLY, HALF TYPED.` → `THE GAP OF ONE BREATH.` → `TWO CHOICES.`

segments.voice: The hadith is in Sahih al-Bukhari. In paraphrase: whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him say what is good, or keep silent. It opens with belief, as if speech is where faith shows up in public. Then it gives two doors, and only two. Good, or silent. There's no third door marked true, so I'll say it anyway. The Qur'an raises the bar. In al-Isra, in Pickthall's translation: "Tell My bondmen to speak that which is kindlier." Not only kind. Kindlier: of two true things, the gentler one. And in al-Baqarah, among the duties of a covenant: "speak kindly to mankind." Mankind, not only friends. Words don't simply vanish, either. Surah Qaf says of each person: "He uttereth no word but there is with him an observer ready." Tradition says that observer is an angel who records; some readers take the verse less as a threat than as a reason to slow down. This is the filter that comes before backbiting and lying. And so the hadith isn't misheard: silence doesn't mean swallowing the truth when it's needed. The Qur'an also calls believers to stand firm for justice, as witnesses for Allah, even against themselves. The silence here is chosen: the word you could have said, left unsaid, because it wasn't good. Courtesy, held in the mouth.
screen: `SAY GOOD, OR KEEP SILENT.` · `FAITH SHOWS UP IN SPEECH.` · `SPEAK THAT WHICH IS KINDLIER.` · `SILENCE AS A CHOICE, NOT A HIDING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one conversation coming up, or one message waiting for a reply, and hear the first thing you'd say. Hold it at the two doors: is it good, and if not, can it become kindlier, or stay unsaid? Breathe in and notice the word, breathe out and let it wait; if you pray, you can hold the words speak that which is kindlier in the quiet.
Adab of speech. The manners of the tongue: say what is good or keep silent, and of two true words, choose the kindlier. Today's word.
Your line: good, or silent. Of two true words, the kindlier. Tomorrow, the adab of eating.

1293.title: Adab of eating
1293.hook: a forgotten bismillah, said late, and the three table instructions taken one at a time
1293.howItsDone: Muslims say bismillah before eating, eat and drink with the right hand, and teach children to eat from the side of the dish nearest them, following the hadith of 'Umar ibn Abi Salamah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the adab of speech, and your line: good, or silent. Today the manners move from the tongue to the table.

Three bites into dinner, a fork stops in midair. The bismillah. Forgotten. Too late now? A hadith in Sunan Abu Dawud and Jami' al-Tirmidhi answers exactly that worry. Whoever forgets the name of Allah at the start, it says, should say it when they remember: in the name of Allah, at its beginning and its end. The name can arrive late and still cover the whole meal. Two days ago, a boy at the Prophet's table heard three short instructions. Today the path sits down with them.
screen: `A FORK IN MIDAIR.` → `THE BISMILLAH, FORGOTTEN.` → `AT ITS BEGINNING AND ITS END.`

segments.voice: The three come from 'Umar ibn Abi Salamah's report in Sahih al-Bukhari. In paraphrase: young man, say the name of Allah, eat with your right hand, and eat from what is in front of you. Each is small enough for a child. The first is bismillah, in the name of Allah. It turns a plate into a gift with a giver, and, as Abu Dawud's hadith says, it can come late. The second is the right hand, which hadith in Sahih Muslim ask for in eating and in drinking. The third is easy to miss: eat from what's near you. At a shared dish, the far side is in someone else's reach. Courtesy turned into geography. Then one more line, from Abu Hurayrah, in Bukhari: the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, never criticized food. If he liked it, he ate it. If he didn't, he left it. So the adab of eating includes the adab of speaking about what you eat. And the Qur'an frames the meal as a gift. In al-Baqarah, in Pickthall's translation: "O ye who believe! Eat of the good things wherewith We have provided you, and render thanks to Allah." The name, even late. The right hand. The near side. No complaints. None of it is elaborate; it's a meal anyone could eat this way tonight.
screen: `BISMILLAH: THE PLATE HAS A GIVER.` · `THE RIGHT HAND.` · `EAT FROM WHAT'S NEAR YOU.` · `NEVER A WORD AGAINST THE FOOD.`

segments.voice: Picture your next meal arriving, at a table or at a desk. If you pray, you can say bismillah, in the name of Allah; if not, simply pause and notice the hands that grew it, carried it, cooked it. See your right hand reach for it, your own side of the plate, and anything not to your taste left quietly, without a word.
Adab of eating. The manners of the table: begin with the name of Allah, eat with the right hand, eat from what's near, and say nothing against the food. Today's word.
Your line: the right hand, the name. Even a late bismillah covers the meal. See you tomorrow.

1294.title: A third for food
1294.hook: one hadith names the worst vessel to fill, then divides it into three
1294.howItsDone: Muslims cite the hadith of the three thirds when they speak of moderation in eating, alongside the Qur'an's "eat and drink, but be not prodigal," and the saying that food for two is enough for three.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the adab of eating: the name, the right hand, the near side. Today, the same table, a different question: how much.

Cups, bags, inboxes, calendars. A person fills a lot of containers in a day. One hadith singles out one vessel as the worst a human being can fill, and it's carried everywhere, all day, right under the ribs. Then the hadith does the math. It divides the vessel into three and gives each part a job, including one part whose job is to stay empty. Today's title is the first of the three.
screen: `THE WORST VESSEL TO FILL.` → `IT DOES THE MATH.` → `ONE PART STAYS EMPTY.`

segments.voice: The hadith is in Jami' al-Tirmidhi, from al-Miqdam ibn Ma'dikarib. In paraphrase, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said: no human being fills a vessel worse than his stomach. A few mouthfuls are enough to keep his back upright. And if he must eat more, then a third for his food, a third for his drink, and a third for his breath. Look at the order. A few mouthfuls first. The thirds are the allowance: if he must. And the last third is kept empty, for breathing. It's room. The Qur'an puts the principle in one line, in al-A'raf, in Pickthall's translation: "eat and drink, but be not prodigal." Both are commanded; the body isn't the enemy. But not wasteful, not past need. This isn't the fast of Ramadan, which has its own days and rules. It's a measure for an ordinary lunch, and not a punishment: nothing in the hadith says hunger is holy. Its picture is a person with a straight back, strong enough to work and to pray. One more hadith, in Sahih al-Bukhari, shows where the empty third can go: food for two is enough for three, and food for three is enough for four. Room is a courtesy too: to the body, and to whoever eats what you didn't.
screen: `THE WORST VESSEL TO FILL.` · `A FEW MOUTHFULS, THEN THIRDS.` · `EAT AND DRINK, BUT BE NOT PRODIGAL.` · `FOOD FOR TWO IS ENOUGH FOR THREE.`

segments.voice: Rest one hand lightly on your stomach and notice what's there, empty, half, full, heavy, without a verdict, then breathe in slowly and feel how much room the breath itself takes: that's the third the hadith keeps empty. Choose the sign that will tell you to stop at your next meal: a slower bite, a sip of water, a breath that comes easily. If food is a hard subject for you, simply stay with the breath; if you pray, you can say alhamdulillah, praise be to Allah, as you set the plate down.
A third for food. The hadith's measure: a few mouthfuls if they're enough, and if not, a third for food, a third for drink, a third for breath. Today's word.
Your line: leave room. The last third is for breath. Tomorrow, the adab of guests.

1295.title: Adab of guests
1295.hook: strangers at Abraham's door, a lamp put out in Medina, and a hadith with two sides
1295.howItsDone: Muslims treat hospitality as part of faith, citing the hadith "let him honor his guest" and the story of Abraham's guests, and teach guests in turn not to overstay or burden their hosts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a third for food, and your line: leave room. Today someone else sits down at your table.

Strangers arrive at Abraham's door. They greet him with peace, and he answers with peace. He doesn't know them, and the Qur'an says he noted that to himself. Then, without asking who they are, he slips away to his household and comes back with a fatted calf, sets it in front of them, and asks why they aren't eating. Surah al-Dhariyat opens the scene, in Pickthall's translation: "Hath the story of Abraham's honoured guests reached thee (O Muhammad)?" You met them on day thirty-eight. Today's adab starts at that door.
screen: `STRANGERS AT ABRAHAM'S DOOR.` → `A FATTED CALF, SET BEFORE THEM.` → `HONORED GUESTS.`

segments.voice: The hadith opens the way the speech hadith did. In Sahih al-Bukhari, in paraphrase, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said: whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honor his guest. Faith, showing up at the door. Another report in Bukhari spells it out: the guest's special due is a day and a night. Hospitality is three days. Anything beyond that is charity. And it isn't right for a guest to stay until he becomes a burden. The host honors; the guest doesn't weigh on the host. Adab runs both ways at the door. Then a story, also in Bukhari, of how far honoring can go. A hungry man came to the Prophet, and his households had nothing but water. A man of the Ansar, the people of Medina, took the guest home. His wife said there was only enough for the children. So they settled the children to sleep, set out the food, and put out the lamp. In the dark they moved their hands as if eating, so their guest could eat his fill and never know. In the morning the Prophet told the man that Allah was pleased with what the two of them had done. The hadith says a verse of al-Hashr came down about them: people who prefer others above themselves, even when they are in need.
screen: `WHOEVER BELIEVES, LET HIM HONOR HIS GUEST.` · `A DAY AND A NIGHT; THREE DAYS.` · `THE GUEST DOESN'T BURDEN THE HOST.` · `THE LAMP PUT OUT IN MEDINA.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you could host, at a table, over tea, or simply by making room for them in a busy day, and see them arriving at your door. What would you set in front of them, not the fanciest thing but the warmest, and how would you make sure they leave light, never feeling like a burden? If you pray, you can make du'a for them by name.
Adab of guests. The manners of the door: the host honors the guest, and the guest takes care not to burden the host. Today's word.
Your line: honor the guest. A good guest doesn't weigh on the host. See you tomorrow, on the road.
